content: Transient tic disorder is a temporary condition characterized by the occurrence of one or more brief, repeated, and involuntary movements or sounds, known as tics. These tics are often difficult to control. Symptoms of Transient Tic Disorder: Children with this condition may exhibit facial tics or tics involving movements of the arms, legs, or other body areas. Tics can include: Repeated, non-rhythmic movements. An overwhelming urge to perform the movement. Brief, jerky movements such as: Blinking. Clenching fists. Curling toes. Flaring nostrils. Grimacing. Jerking the arms. Kicking. Opening the mouth. Raising the eyebrows. Shrugging shoulders. Sticking out the tongue. These tics often resemble nervous behaviors and tend to worsen with stress. They do not occur during sleep. Sounds may also accompany the tics, including: Clicking. Grunting. Hissing. Moaning. Sniffing. Snorting. Squealing. Throat clearing. Causes of Transient Tic Disorder: This condition is common in children. The causes can be either physical or psychological in nature. It may represent a mild form of Tourette syndrome. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Consult a healthcare provider if you are concerned about transient tic disorder, especially if the tics persist or interfere with the child’s daily life. If there is uncertainty about whether the movements are tics or seizures, contact a healthcare provider immediately. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider should rule out physical causes before diagnosing transient tic disorder. To confirm the diagnosis, the child must have experienced tics almost daily for at least four weeks but less than one year. Other conditions, such as anxiety, attention deficit disorder, myoclonus, obsessive-compulsive disorder, epilepsy, and focal dystonia, may need to be excluded. Treatment Options: Healthcare providers often advise family members not to draw attention to the tics initially, as unwanted attention can exacerbate the condition. If the tics are severe enough to cause problems at school or work, behavioral techniques and medications may be beneficial. Medical Care for Transient Tic Disorder: Directions to hospitals or clinics specializing in the treatment of transient tic disorder can be sought for further assistance. Prognosis: Simple childhood tics typically resolve over a period of months. Possible Complications: Complications are rare. However, a chronic motor or vocal tic disorder may develop in some cases.
